messages.text: I accept the wake-clearance rule and the 62 % completeness flag without modification; they keep the weekly bulletin honest without forcing us to discard a season of data. For the gauge variable you have left open, each site will carry a 20-inch standard rain gauge with a self-cleaning wiper at 1.0 m above mown grass, supplemented in winter by a graduated-cylinder secondary read at 02:00 to capture frozen accumulation that no tipping-bucket threshold can resolve. The failure this guards against is unglamorous but persistent: a single evergreen bough overhanging the inlet by only 15° intercepts enough light-rain droplets to shave roughly 15 % off every event, so a true monthly total of 60 mm is logged as ≈51 mm and the neighborhood's comparison column quietly trends low against the NOAA station. I therefore require the same 360° horizon-sketch at installation for the rain inlet, with any bough within 30° of the rim annotated and a pruning-or-relocation note entered before the first forecast snowfall.

messages.text: I adopt the bough-annotation rule and the 02:00 graduated-cylinder procedure; without that winter secondary read a snowpack that hoards and later releases four millimetres overnight would surface as a phantom 0.4 mm/hr rate in the hourly log, exactly the kind of artifact your pruning note is meant to eliminate. For the pressure variable you listed but have not yet instrumented, each site will carry a sealed aneroid module (0.1 hPa resolution) calibrated monthly against a NIST-traceable portable barometer, and every reading is reduced to mean-sea level using the site's surveyed elevation and a temperature-corrected lapse rate before the weekly comparison column is populated. The failure this guards against is mundane but diagnostic: if Site 3, sitting eighteen metres above Site 1, simply logs raw station pressure and the compiler forgets the MSL correction, the bulletin shows a persistent ≈1.5 hPa "high" at Site 3 that mimics a blocked-ridge signature and poisons the cross-site coherence check. I therefore require that any inter-site pressure spread exceeding 0.5 hPa after MSL reduction triggers an automatic elevation-recording audit—a repeat GPS survey of the affected site—rather than a silent averaging across the six columns.
